az_bikini_wall.blurb: A short sandstone cliff band beside Highway 89A just north of Grasshopper Point in Sedona, holding a tight cluster of eight boulder problems. This is a venue for strong climbers: the problems start around V7 and climb into the low teens, with several sitting at V9 to V11. Nothing here is a warm-up. The wall stays shaded for most of the day, which helps on warm afternoons. The walk from the roadside pullouts is short and heads downhill, so the wall comes into view on your right.

az_seeds_n_stems_boulder.blurb: The southernmost block at the Anvil Boulders near Sedona, really a pair of boulders divided by a wide crack. Eight sandstone problems cover a friendly range: a few easy ones from VB to V2, a cluster around V5, and a single hard V7 for the top end. The Anvils as a whole have a short walk in and are well regarded for their quality lines. Because of the elevation they make a decent choice for getting out in the shoulder seasons.

az_3_jolly_roger.blurb: A small bouldering zone in Middle Elden, the canyon that splits Mount Elden north to south above Flagstaff, at roughly 7,400 ft. Eight problems range from an easy V0 up to the V10 to V11 range, with most falling between V0 and V6 and a few much harder lines near the top. Canyon walls throw shade, especially on the west side late in the day. Middle Elden has plenty of awkward landings, so bring several pads and a few friends to spot. It also has a reputation as a good winter spot.

az_bad_ass_roof.blurb: A roof-style bouldering spot in Howard Draw, next to Priest Draw outside Flagstaff, at about 7,000 ft. Eight problems run from an easy V1 up to V10, with the bulk between V4 and V8. The draw has a gentle, quieter feel than its neighbor, though the roof can pull a crowd on weekends. The trail leads out the draw a few minutes beyond a landmark island, then the roof sits on the right, a little up the hillside, around ten minutes from the parking area.

az_lost_wall_3.blurb: A tall cliff of about 300 ft on the Lower Highway of Mount Lemmon in the Santa Catalina Mountains near Tucson, at around 5,600 ft. It is not a sport crag: the eight routes are mostly trad, with a single aid line, running from 5.6 through 5.9 and 5.10 to a 5.11. Big roofs, plates, thin edges and cracks make it a good stop for crack climbers, and the rock is good to excellent. Some anchors are tired, so plan accordingly. The Lower Highway crags are at their best in winter.

az_8_one_day_wall.blurb: A small wall at the right-hand end of the Chessman Area in Bear Canyon on Mount Lemmon, near Tucson. Seven moderate routes mix bolted and gear lines, from 5.6 up to 5.9, with most sitting at 5.7 and below, so newer climbers have plenty to work with. The wall catches shade in the morning. The walk in is steep and tiring in both directions, so expect more effort than the grades suggest. The wider Chessman Area is low in elevation and close to the road, which makes for an easy day out.

az_lucky_s_boulder.blurb: A small boulder in Gandalf's Gorge, part of the Aspen Trail Boulders high on Mount Lemmon beyond Summerhaven, at roughly 7,100 ft. It holds seven problems: a few moderate lines around V4 and V5, then several hard ones between V9 and V11. It sits on the right side of the streambed and is easy to spot from the Warm Up Boulder. The surrounding zone, with its stream and trees, is known as a summer bouldering destination, and a day plan among its walls can keep you in the shade all day.
